stories.bridge: Popper's criterion is the sharpest tool in the epistemology kit. Now let's learn to wield it — on science, on technology, and on your own beliefs.
stories.hook: In 1934, Karl Popper published a book arguing that science can never prove anything — only disprove.
stories.narrative: Popper was a young Viennese philosopher watching his contemporaries — Marxists, Freudians, astrologers — claim scientific status for theories that could explain everything and therefore predicted nothing. In 'Logik der Forschung' (The Logic of Scientific Discovery), published in 1934, he proposed the demarcation criterion that made him famous: a theory is scientific not if it can be verified, but if it can be falsified — if it sticks its neck out and risks being wrong. His hero was Einstein, who in 1915 had predicted exactly how much starlight would bend near the sun; when Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition confirmed it, the theory survived a test that could have killed it. That, Popper said, is what science looks like: bold conjectures, severe tests. The criterion reshaped philosophy of science and leaked into everything — it's the logic underneath the hypothesis test, the A/B test, and the scientific method as taught in schools. Popper spent the rest of his long life (he died in 1994) defending the open society against historicism and totalizing ideologies, arguing that the same fallibilism that powers science should govern politics: we can't know we're right, so we build institutions that let us correct our errors. For the technologist, falsificationism is a working discipline, not just philosophy: state your claim so it can fail, run the test that could kill it, and update. The hypothesis that survives is the one you've actually earned. Popper's criterion took hits — Kuhn, Feyerabend, and the historians showed science is messier than the logic — but as a working discipline it survives everywhere: the severe test is still the gold standard, from particle physics to A/B testing. For the technologist, the takeaway is practical, not philosophical: design the test that could prove you wrong, and run it first. The beliefs that survive are the only ones you've earned.
stories.title: The story behind falsification
verifiedClaims: The criterion demarcates science by falsifiability, not verifiability
Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition tested Einstein's prediction

stories.bridge: Kuhn showed that science advances by revolution, not accumulation. Now let's trace those revolutions — from 1800 to the present — and learn to spot the next one.

figures.name: Thomas Kuhn
figures.role: Physicist and historian; author of 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962)

stories.hook: In 1962, Thomas Kuhn argued that science doesn't progress — it revolts.
stories.narrative: Kuhn was a physicist turned historian who had an epiphany reading Aristotle: the old texts weren't stupid, they were coherent — within a different worldview. In 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962), he argued that science doesn't advance by steady accumulation but by long periods of 'normal science' — puzzle-solving within a shared paradigm — punctuated by crises, when anomalies pile up and a revolution installs a new paradigm. The examples were the great overturnings: Copernicus displacing Ptolemy, Lavoisier displacing phlogiston, Einstein displacing Newton. The radical claim was incommensurability: paradigms don't just add facts, they change what counts as a fact — scientists across a revolution, Kuhn said, 'live in different worlds.' The book became one of the most cited academic works of the century, and 'paradigm shift' escaped into business jargon, much to Kuhn's annoyance. Philosophers argued with him for decades — Popper most fiercely — but working scientists recognized the pattern: the long grind, the mounting anomalies, the sudden flip. For the technologist, Kuhn's lens is a way to read your own field: deep learning's 2012 revolution had all the markers — the anomalies accumulating against the old paradigm, the sudden reorganization of what counted as progress. Normal science is where careers are built; revolutions are where they're made. Learn to tell which phase you're in. The book's most controversial claim — incommensurability, the idea that rival paradigms can't fully communicate — drew fire from Popper and others, but the core pattern stuck: normal science, crisis, revolution. Watch for it in your own field: the anomalies accumulating at the edges, the young researchers ignoring the old rules, the sudden flip. Kuhn gave you the diagnostic; the history of science in this module gives you the case studies. Normal science builds careers; revolutions make them. Learn to tell which phase you're in.
stories.title: The story behind the paradigm shift
verifiedClaims: Kuhn published 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' in 1962
It introduced paradigm, normal science, and incommensurability
The phrase 'paradigm shift' entered general language from the book

stories.bridge: Smith's pin factory is still the clearest explanation of why specialization works. Now let's learn the economics — markets, costs, incentives — that every engineer operates inside.

figures.name: Adam Smith
figures.role: Moral philosopher; author of 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776)

stories.hook: In March 1776, Adam Smith published the book that invented economics.
stories.narrative: Smith was a Glasgow professor of moral philosophy who spent a decade writing 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations,' published in March 1776 — the same year as American independence, a coincidence he would have appreciated. The book's opening is its most famous passage: a pin factory, where ten workers dividing the labor — one drawing wire, one straightening, one cutting — produce thousands of pins a day, while a lone craftsman might make a handful. Division of labor, specialization, the productivity miracle: the founding insight of economics, stated before the economics existed. The book's deeper argument was about the system that lets the pin factory work: markets coordinating strangers through prices, the 'invisible hand' aligning self-interest with the public good — a phrase Smith used sparingly but posterity made famous. He was no naive celebrant: the book warns about monopolies, the misery of the laborer, and the need for public goods like education. But the core stands: wealth comes not from gold but from productive organization. For the engineer, Smith is the background radiation of every cost discussion you'll ever have — specialization, trade-offs, incentives, the division of labor that makes your own team productive. When this module teaches markets and costs, it's teaching Smith's 1776 machinery. The pin factory is still running; it's just been automated. Smith's pin factory had a shadow he acknowledged: the worker confined to one operation becomes, in his words, "as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become" — which is why he argued for public education. The Wealth of Nations is subtler than its slogans. In this module you'll learn the machinery — markets, costs, incentives — but read Smith whole: the founder of economics worried about what the division of labor does to the laborer.
stories.title: The story behind The Wealth of Nations
verifiedClaims: 'The Wealth of Nations' was published in March 1776
It opens with the pin-factory analysis of division of labor
Smith was a professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow

stories.bridge: Feynman showed that explaining clearly is the ultimate test of understanding. Now let's learn technical writing as he practiced it — no jargon, no hiding, no mercy for confusion.
stories.hook: In 1961, Caltech asked Richard Feynman to teach freshman physics — and he reinvented explanation.
stories.narrative: Feynman was already a legend — a Manhattan Project veteran, a Nobel laureate-to-be (1965, for quantum electrodynamics), famous for his bongo drums and his disdain for pretension. When Caltech asked him to overhaul the introductory physics course, he agreed on one condition: he would teach it his way, from scratch, with no deference to the textbook order. For two years, 1961 to 1963, he lectured to freshmen — and to a growing crowd of faculty and graduate students who snuck in to watch. Robert Leighton and Matthew Sands turned the recordings and notes into 'The Feynman Lectures on Physics,' published in 1964: three volumes that have never gone out of print and are now free online. The lectures' secret wasn't simplification — Feynman never dumbed anything down. It was reconstruction: he rebuilt each topic from first principles, in his own order, with his own analogies, refusing to hide behind formalism. The famous line about the lectures is that they were too hard for freshmen and perfect for everyone else. For technical writing, Feynman is the gold standard and the method: understand so deeply you can rebuild it simply, use the concrete before the abstract, and never let jargon do the work of thought. This module's standard is Feynman's — if you can't explain it to a smart freshman, you don't understand it yet. He proved it weekly, in front of hundreds, with chalk. The lectures' famous difficulty is the point: Feynman refused to simplify, only to clarify — and generations of physicists learned that clarity is the harder achievement. His technique for learning — explain it simply, find the gaps, repeat — is this module's method for writing. If your explanation needs jargon to stand up, it doesn't stand up. Rebuild it until a freshman could follow. Clarity is the achievement; jargon is the hiding place.
stories.title: The story behind the Feynman Lectures
verifiedClaims: Feynman taught the Caltech introductory course 1961–1963
'The Feynman Lectures on Physics' was published in 1964
Leighton and Sands produced the volumes from the lectures
